events.dateNotes: Twentieth year of Artaxerxes I (Neh 2:1), 445/444 BC; the wall was finished in 52 days (Neh 6:15). Ussher, Annals §1226-1234, has Nehemiah's news in 455 BC (9th month, 20th year) and the wall built in 454 BC; this dataset keeps the standard date.

people.role: Brought the report that led Nehemiah to go; later put in charge of Jerusalem

events.name: Ezra Reads the Law at the Water Gate
events.description: On the first day of the seventh month the people gather in the square before the Water Gate and ask Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses. From morning until midday he reads it, and the Levites give the sense so that all understand. The people weep, then keep the Feast of Booths with joy, and a solemn assembly follows.
events.dateNotes: Nehemiah 8:1-2 gives the first day of the seventh month, soon after the wall was finished. Standard dating follows the wall (445 BC, Artaxerxes' twentieth year), so c. 445/444 BC. Ussher, Annals §1238-1239, puts the reading in 454 BC, the year he finishes the wall (his Artaxerxes reigns from 474/5 BC, about nine years earlier than the standard reckoning). Some scholars place Ezra after Nehemiah.

events.name: Malachi's Ministry
events.description: Malachi, the last of the prophets of the Old Testament, rebukes a restored community that has grown careless: priests offer blemished sacrifices, tithes are withheld and marriages are broken faith. He promises a messenger to prepare the way of the Lord and ends with the promise of Elijah to come before the great day of the LORD.
events.dateNotes: The book is undated. Its abuses match the time of Nehemiah's second term, so c. 430 BC is an estimate; scholars place Malachi between c. 480 and 430 BC. Ussher (Annals §1305) has him in 416 BC, contemporary with Nehemiah's second return.

events.name: Alexander Conquers the Persian Empire
events.description: Alexander of Macedon defeats Persia at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela and rules an empire from Greece to India. Judea passes from Persian to Greek rule and, after his death in 323 BC, to the rival Ptolemies and Seleucids (1 Macc 1:1-9). Daniel's vision of the he-goat is traditionally read of these events (Dan 8:5-8, 21-22; 11:3-4).
events.dateNotes: Campaign 334-323 BC; Alexander died at Babylon in June 323 BC. Reading the Daniel passages as Alexander is traditional.

events.name: Septuagint Translation Begun in Alexandria
events.description: Tradition holds that at the request of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, seventy-two Jewish scholars from Jerusalem translated the Law into Greek at Alexandria. The Greek Old Testament that grew from this work, the Septuagint, became the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of most New Testament writers who quote Scripture.
events.dateNotes: Tradition, from the Letter of Aristeas (a legendary account, probably written in the second century BC). Ussher, Annals §2774 (after Epiphanius), dates the translation by 72 translators to the seventh year of Ptolemy Philadelphus, 277 BC. Historians accept that the Pentateuch was translated in Alexandria in the third century BC, c. 280-250 BC; the other books followed over the next two centuries.

events.name: Maccabean Revolt
events.description: After Antiochus IV desecrates the temple and bans the Law, the priest Mattathias refuses to sacrifice at Modein and raises a revolt (1 Macc 2). His son Judas wins a string of victories, retakes Jerusalem and rededicates the temple in December 165 BC on Ussher's dating (1 Macc 4:36-59). Judas falls at Elasa in 161 BC (Ussher).
events.dateNotes: The temple was desecrated on 15 Kislev 145 of the kingdom of the Greeks (1 Macc 1:54): 167 BC, Ussher, Annals §3347. Judas fell in 152 of that era (1 Macc 9:3): 161 BC on Ussher (§3528-3532). Standard dating counts the era a year later: rededication 164 BC and Judas's death 160 BC. 1-2 Maccabees are canonical for Catholics and Orthodox and among the Apocrypha for Protestants.

people.role: Brother and later leader of the revolt
Brother and later leader of the revolt

events.name: Antiochus IV Desecrates the Temple
events.description: Antiochus IV Epiphanes forbids circumcision, the Sabbath and the Law, and in December 167 BC an altar to Zeus is set up on the altar of burnt offering in the Jerusalem temple. Daniel 11:31 is often read as pointing to these acts. The outrage leads directly to the Maccabean Revolt.
events.dateNotes: Standard historical dating from 1 and 2 Maccabees (1 Macc 1:54, 15 Kislev, 145 of the Seleucid era = December 167 BC). Maccabees is not in the KJV text used here; the Daniel link is a traditional reading, not a certainty.

people.role: Seleucid king who ordered the desecration

events.name: Rededication of the Temple
events.description: On 25 Kislev, three years after its desecration, Judas Maccabeus cleanses the temple, builds a new altar and restores the daily offerings with eight days of celebration (1 Macc 4:36-59; 2 Macc 10:1-8). The feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) that remembers it is named in John 10:22.
events.dateNotes: 25 Kislev 148 of the kingdom of the Greeks (1 Macc 4:52). Ussher, Annals §3417-3421, places it in 165 BC; this dataset follows Ussher. Standard dating: December 164 BC.

events.name: Pompey Takes Jerusalem
events.description: The Roman general Pompey, called in to settle a quarrel between the Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, besieges the temple mount for three months and storms it. He enters the Holy of Holies but leaves the treasury untouched. Judea becomes a Roman tributary, the political setting of the Gospels.
events.dateNotes: Standard historical dating from Josephus (Antiquities 14.57-71; War 1.141-154): 63 BC.

events.name: Herod Made King of Judea by Rome
events.description: Driven from Judea by the Parthians, Herod goes to Rome, where the Senate, with the support of Mark Antony and Octavian, names him king of the Jews. He takes Jerusalem with Roman help in 37 BC and rules until his death c. 4 BC. This is the "Herod the king" of the birth narratives.
events.dateNotes: Standard historical dating from Josephus (Antiquities 14.381-389; 14.468-491): appointed 40 BC, took Jerusalem 37 BC.

people.role: Octavian, who backed the Senate's decree

events.name: Herod Begins Rebuilding the Temple
events.description: Herod the Great begins to rebuild and enlarge the Jerusalem temple in the eighteenth year of his reign, with the sanctuary itself finished in about eighteen months and the surrounding courts and porches continuing for decades. The Jews tell Jesus the work has been going on forty-six years.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §5938: in the eighteenth year of Herod, counted from the death of Antigonus in 37 BC, he announced the rebuilding: 19 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 15.380; some date it 20/19 BC). John 2:20 (46 years) would then fall in AD 27/28; the figure counts building in progress and is not a precise anchor.

people.role: Began the rebuilding of the temple

events.name: Birth of Jesus
events.description: In Bethlehem, Mary gives birth to Jesus, announced by angels to shepherds and honored by magi from the east; Matthew and Luke present him as Messiah, son of David, and Immanuel. The Gospels root his birth in Micah's prophecy of a ruler from Bethlehem, opening the fulfillment of Israel's long story.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §6057, headed 5 BC (Quirinius' census, Luke 2:1-7; §6049-6056). Matthew places the birth before the death of Herod the Great (Matt 2:1, 19), whom Ussher dates to 4 BC (§6080), so the year agrees with Scripture's order. Many modern scholars give 6-4 BC.

people.role: His census decree brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem (Luke 2:1)

events.name: Annunciation to Mary
events.description: The angel Gabriel announces to Mary at Nazareth that she will conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear a son named Jesus, and Mary consents. She then visits her relative Elizabeth, who is six months pregnant with John. Matthew tells of the angel's message to Joseph in a dream.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §6039: 5 BC, in the sixth month after John was conceived (Luke 1:26, 36), nine months before the birth of Jesus. Scripture gives no year.

events.name: Birth of John the Baptist
events.description: Elizabeth bears a son to the aged priest Zechariah, who regains his speech when he writes that the child's name is John. Zechariah's song (the Benedictus) foretells that the child will prepare the way of the Lord.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §6043: 5 BC, about six months before the birth of Jesus (Luke 1:26, 36). Scripture gives no year.

events.name: Visit of the Magi and Flight into Egypt
events.description: Magi from the east follow a star to Jerusalem and Bethlehem, worship the child Jesus and, warned in a dream, go home another way. Herod the Great orders the killing of the boys of Bethlehem aged two and under; Joseph, warned by an angel, takes Mary and the child to Egypt until Herod's death and then settles in Nazareth.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §6060, §6064: the Magi come and the flight to Egypt falls in 4 BC, before Herod's death (late 4 BC, §6080; Matt 2:1, 19); the return to Nazareth after Herod's death is headed 3 BC (§6084; Matt 2:19-23), so the event runs 4 BC to 3 BC. Matthew does not say the Magi were three, or kings. The massacre is recorded only by Matthew.

events.name: Presentation of Jesus in the Temple
events.description: Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph bring Jesus to the Temple to present him to the Lord and offer the sacrifice of the poor. The aged Simeon takes him in his arms and blesses God (the Nunc Dimittis), and the prophetess Anna speaks of him to all who looked for redemption.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §6061: headed 4 BC, on the fortieth day after the birth (Luke 2:22; Lev 12:2-4); the birth being late in 5 BC in the Annals, the presentation falls early in 4 BC. Was 5 BC.

events.name: Boy Jesus in the Temple
events.description: At twelve, Jesus goes up to Jerusalem with Mary and Joseph for Passover and stays behind; after three days they find him in the Temple among the teachers, who are astonished at his understanding. He returns with them to Nazareth and grows in wisdom and stature. It is the last time Joseph appears in the Gospels.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §6185: the Passover of AD 8, in the twelfth year of his age (Luke 2:41-42), on a 5 BC birth.

events.name: Baptism of Jesus
events.description: Jesus is baptized by John in the Jordan River, where the Spirit descends like a dove and a voice from heaven declares him the beloved Son. The moment inaugurates his public ministry; John himself is independently attested by the historian Josephus, who records his baptizing movement and death.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §6288: AD 27, early in the year, after John's ministry began in the fifteenth year of Tiberius reckoned from his co-regency (Luke 3:1; John begins October AD 26, §6280-6283). Luke 3:23 says 'about thirty'; on Ussher's birth in late 5 BC he is about 31, which Scripture allows. The first Passover of the ministry is AD 30 (John 2:13, 20; §6302), so Ussher leaves about three years between baptism and that Passover; John 1:19-2:13 reads as continuous, a tension the Annals do not remove. Was AD 29 (Tiberius' fifteenth year counted from his accession in AD 14, giving AD 28/29); some place it in AD 26.

people.role: Emperor in whose fifteenth year John began his ministry (Luke 3:1)
Tetrarch named in Luke 3:1 as ruling at the time

events.name: Water Turned to Wine
events.description: At a wedding in Cana of Galilee, prompted by his mother Mary, Jesus turned water in six stone purification jars into choice wine. John alone records this first sign, which revealed Jesus' glory to his disciples and inaugurated his public ministry with an image of messianic abundance.
events.dateNotes: John 2:1-11. Ussher, Annals §6301: AD 30. Placed by Ussher just before the first Passover (John 2:13).

events.name: Healing of the Official's Son
events.description: Jesus heals a royal official's son in Capernaum from a distance.
events.dateNotes: John 4:46-54; second sign in John (John 4:54). Ussher, Annals §6316: AD 30. After the stay at Sychar (John 4:35).

events.name: Sermon on the Mount
events.description: On a Galilean hillside, Jesus delivers his most famous teaching, opening with the Beatitudes and pressing the Law to its deepest intent on anger, love of enemies, and prayer, including the Lord's Prayer. Matthew presents him as the authoritative teacher of a righteousness surpassing that of the scribes.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 5-7; compare Luke 6:20-49. Ussher, Annals §6338: AD 31. Luke places the Sermon on the Plain after the withered hand and the choosing of the Twelve (Luke 6:6-20).

events.name: Great Catch of Fish
events.description: Jesus directs a miraculous catch of fish on the Sea of Galilee.
events.dateNotes: Luke 5:1-11; calling of the first disciples. Ussher, Annals §6325: AD 31.

events.name: Healing of a Demon-Possessed Man in Capernaum
events.description: Jesus casts out an unclean spirit in the Capernaum synagogue.
events.dateNotes: Mark 1:21-28; Luke 4:31-37. Ussher, Annals §6319: AD 31.

events.name: Healing of Peter's Mother-in-Law
events.description: Jesus heals Simon Peter's mother-in-law of a fever.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 8:14-15; Mark 1:29-31; Luke 4:38-39. Ussher, Annals §6320: AD 31.

events.name: Cleansing of a Leper
events.description: Jesus heals a man with leprosy by touching him.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 8:1-4; Mark 1:40-45; Luke 5:12-16. Ussher, Annals §6327: AD 31.

events.name: Healing of the Paralytic
events.description: In Capernaum, four friends lowered a paralyzed man through the roof to reach Jesus, who first forgave his sins and then commanded him to walk. Matthew, Mark, and Luke record the miracle, which joined Jesus' power to heal with his authority to forgive; Capernaum excavations reveal the crowded basalt houses such a scene assumes.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 9:1-8; Mark 2:1-12; Luke 5:17-26. Ussher, Annals §6328: AD 31.

events.name: Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
events.description: Jesus heals a man who had been an invalid for 38 years.
events.dateNotes: John 5:1-17; on a Sabbath. Ussher takes the unnamed feast of John 5:1 as the second Passover (some take it as Tabernacles or Purim). Ussher, Annals §6332: AD 31.

events.name: Healing of a Withered Hand
events.description: Jesus heals a man's withered hand on the Sabbath in the synagogue.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 12:9-14; Mark 3:1-6; Luke 6:6-11. Ussher, Annals §6333: AD 31.

events.name: Healing of the Centurion's Servant
events.description: A Roman centurion in Capernaum asked Jesus to heal his dying servant, insisting a word from a distance would suffice. Jesus marveled that he had found no such faith in Israel and healed the servant without entering the house; Luke adds that this Gentile officer had built the town's synagogue.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 8:5-13; Luke 7:1-10. Ussher, Annals §6339: AD 31.

events.name: Raising of the Widow's Son at Nain
events.description: Meeting a funeral procession at the gate of Nain, Jesus was moved by a widow who had lost her only son, touched the bier, and restored the young man to life. Found only in Luke, the miracle echoes Elijah's raising of the widow's son at Zarephath and led the crowd to hail a great prophet.
events.dateNotes: Luke 7:11-17; only in Luke. Ussher, Annals §6340: AD 31.

events.name: Calming the Storm
events.description: When a sudden squall threatened to swamp the disciples' boat on the Sea of Galilee, Jesus rose from sleep and stilled wind and waves with a word. All three synoptic gospels record the awed question of who this could be; a first-century fishing boat excavated from the lake's mud vividly illustrates the scene.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 8:23-27; Mark 4:35-41; Luke 8:22-25. Ussher, Annals §6347: AD 31.

events.name: Healing of the Gerasene Demoniac
events.description: In the Decapolis east of the Sea of Galilee, Jesus freed a tomb-dwelling man possessed by a legion of demons, which entered a herd of pigs and perished in the sea. Sent home rather than allowed to follow, the man became the first herald of Jesus in Gentile lands; manuscripts vary between Gerasenes, Gadarenes, and Gergesenes.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 8:28-34; Mark 5:1-20; Luke 8:26-39. Ussher, Annals §6348: AD 31.

events.name: Healing of the Woman with the Issue of Blood
events.description: A woman touches Jesus' garment and is healed after 12 years of bleeding.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 9:20-22; Mark 5:25-34; Luke 8:43-48. Ussher, Annals §6349-6351: AD 31.

events.name: Raising of Jairus' Daughter
events.description: Jairus, a synagogue leader, begged Jesus to save his dying daughter, and though word came that she had died, Jesus took her hand and raised her. Mark preserves the original Aramaic command, Talitha koum, and all three synoptics interweave the story with the healing of the hemorrhaging woman.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 9:18-26; Mark 5:21-43; Luke 8:40-56. Ussher, Annals §6351: AD 31.

events.name: Healing of Two Blind Men
events.description: Jesus restores sight to two blind men who follow him crying for mercy.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 9:27-31. Ussher, Annals §6352: AD 31. Matthew sets it directly after Jairus' daughter.

events.name: Healing of a Mute Man
events.description: Jesus casts out a demon and the mute man speaks.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 9:32-34. Ussher, Annals §6353: AD 31.

events.name: Feeding of the 5,000
events.description: With five loaves and two fish from the crowd, Jesus fed thousands beside the Sea of Galilee, with twelve baskets left over. It is the only miracle of his ministry recorded in all four gospels, recalling the manna in the wilderness and prompting John's discourse on Jesus as the bread of life.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 14:13-21; Mark 6:30-44; Luke 9:10-17; John 6:1-15. Only miracle in all four Gospels. At the Passover of John 6:4 (Ussher's third). Ussher, Annals §6367: AD 32.

people.role: Pointed out the boy with loaves and fish (John 6:8)
Asked by Jesus where to buy bread (John 6:5-7)

events.name: Walking on Water
events.description: In the night after feeding the multitude, Jesus came to his storm-battered disciples walking across the Sea of Galilee. Matthew, Mark, and John record the event, with Matthew adding Peter's brief walk and sinking; Jesus' reassurance, echoing the divine I am, moved the disciples to worship him as God's Son.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 14:22-33; Mark 6:45-52; John 6:16-21. The night after the feeding of the 5,000. Ussher, Annals §6367-6368: AD 32.

events.name: Healing of the Syrophoenician Woman's Daughter
events.description: Jesus heals a Gentile woman's demon-possessed daughter.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 15:21-28; Mark 7:24-30. Ussher, Annals §6370: AD 32.

events.name: Healing of a Deaf and Mute Man
events.description: Jesus heals a deaf man with a speech impediment in the Decapolis.
events.dateNotes: Mark 7:31-37. Ussher, Annals §6371: AD 32.

events.name: Feeding of the 4,000
events.description: In the largely Gentile Decapolis region, Jesus fed a crowd that had stayed with him three days, multiplying seven loaves and a few fish with seven baskets remaining. Recorded by Matthew and Mark as distinct from the earlier feeding, it signals that the messianic banquet extends beyond Israel to the nations.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 15:32-39; Mark 8:1-10. Ussher, Annals §6373: AD 32.

events.name: Healing of a Blind Man at Bethsaida
events.description: Jesus heals a blind man in two stages at Bethsaida.
events.dateNotes: Mark 8:22-26; only in Mark. Ussher, Annals §6377: AD 32.

events.name: Transfiguration
events.description: On a high mountain, Peter, James, and John saw Jesus transfigured in dazzling glory, conversing with Moses and Elijah as a voice from the cloud declared him the beloved Son. All three synoptics record the scene, which links law and prophets to Jesus; 2 Peter appeals to it as eyewitness testimony.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 17:1-13; Mark 9:2-13; Luke 9:28-36. Six (Luke: about eight) days after Peter's confession (Matt 17:1; Luke 9:28). Ussher, Annals §6379: AD 32.

events.name: Healing of a Boy with a Demon
events.description: Jesus casts out a demon the disciples could not.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 17:14-21; Mark 9:14-29; Luke 9:37-43. Ussher, Annals §6380: AD 32.

events.name: Coin in the Fish's Mouth
events.description: Jesus instructs Peter to find a coin in a fish's mouth for Temple tax.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 17:24-27; only in Matthew. Ussher, Annals §6382: AD 32.

events.name: Healing of the Man Born Blind
events.description: Jesus anointed the eyes of a man blind from birth and sent him to wash in the Pool of Siloam, where he received sight. John alone tells the story, following the man's bold testimony under interrogation; the stepped first-century pool itself has been uncovered in recent Jerusalem excavations.
events.dateNotes: John 9:1-41; extended discourse on spiritual blindness. Follows the Feast of Tabernacles (John 7:2, 37; autumn AD 32) and precedes the Feast of Dedication (John 10:22). Ussher, Annals §6394: AD 32.

events.name: Healing of a Crippled Woman
events.description: Jesus heals a woman bent over for 18 years on the Sabbath.
events.dateNotes: Luke 13:10-17; only in Luke. Within Luke's journey to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51-19:28). Ussher, Annals §6407-6408 places it after the Tabernacles of AD 32 and on the way to the Dedication (Dec AD 32), yet the printed heading over §6399-6452 reads AD 33; the year is kept at AD 32 (winter AD 32/33) and flagged approximate.

events.name: Death of John the Baptist
events.description: Herod Antipas has John imprisoned for condemning his marriage to Herodias, his brother Philip's former wife. At Herod's birthday banquet Herodias's daughter pleases him with a dance and, prompted by her mother, asks for John's head, which is carried in on a platter. John's disciples bury the body and tell Jesus. Josephus names the fortress of Machaerus as the prison.
events.dateNotes: Matt 14:1-12; Mark 6:17-29. Ussher dates the imprisonment to AD 30 (§6311, John 3:24) and the beheading to AD 32, before the feeding of the 5,000 (Matt 14:12-13). Machaerus is Josephus's account, not the Gospels'. Ussher, Annals §6362: AD 32.

people.role: Tetrarch who imprisoned and killed John
Wife of Antipas who demanded John's death
Heard of John's death and withdrew

events.name: Crucifixion
events.description: Condemned under Pontius Pilate, Jesus is crucified at Golgotha outside Jerusalem at Passover, and the Gospels present his death as an atoning sacrifice foretold by the prophets. Pilate is attested by an inscription found at Caesarea, and a crucified man's heel bone from Jerusalem confirms the Roman practice.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: Friday 3 April AD 33; AD 30 (Friday 7 April) is the main alternative. Both fall within Pilate's prefecture (AD 26-36). Ussher, Annals §6467-6479: AD 33.

events.name: Resurrection
events.description: On the third day, women find Jesus' tomb empty and meet the risen Lord, who then appears to his disciples over forty days. Paul preserves an early creed listing eyewitnesses of the resurrection, the event Christians confess as death's defeat and the firstfruits of the new creation.
events.dateNotes: The third day after the crucifixion (Ussher: Sunday 5 April AD 33); AD 33 (AD 30 on the main alternative). Ussher, Annals §6484: AD 33.

events.name: Ascension
events.description: Forty days after the resurrection, Jesus blesses his disciples on the Mount of Olives and is taken up into heaven, commissioning them as witnesses to the ends of the earth. Angels declare he will return as he departed, framing the church's mission between promise and hope.
events.dateNotes: Forty days after the resurrection (Acts 1:3). Ussher, Annals §6493, §6506: AD 33.

events.name: Pentecost
events.description: On the feast of Pentecost, fifty days after Passover, the Holy Spirit descends on the disciples with rushing wind and tongues of fire, and Peter's sermon draws about three thousand into the newborn church. Falling on Shavuot, the harvest festival, the event launches the gospel's spread from Jerusalem.
events.dateNotes: Fifty days after the Passover of the crucifixion year (Acts 2:1; Lev 23:15-16); Ussher: 24 May AD 33 (AD 30 on the main alternative). Ussher, Annals §6510: AD 33.

people.role: Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)

events.name: Stoning of Stephen
events.description: Stephen, one of the seven (Acts 6:5), is arrested, defends himself before the council and is stoned outside the city while Saul consents; he becomes the first Christian martyr (Acts 6:8-8:2).
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6518-6521: late AD 33, soon after Pentecost; the great persecution and scattering follow in AD 34 (6524, Acts 8:1). Scripture gives no year. Earlier row had AD 35; some place it AD 31-36.

events.name: Healing of a Man with Dropsy
events.description: Jesus heals a man with dropsy (edema) on the Sabbath.
events.dateNotes: Luke 14:1-6; only in Luke. Within Luke's journey to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51-19:28). Ussher, Annals §6411-6412 lies under the heading AD 33 but before the Dedication paragraph (§6422, December); year kept at AD 33 and flagged approximate.

events.name: Raising of Lazarus
events.description: At Bethany, Jesus called Lazarus out of the tomb four days after his death, having declared to Martha that he is the resurrection and the life. This climactic sign, recorded only in John, drew crowds toward Jerusalem and hardened the authorities' resolve to put Jesus to death.
events.dateNotes: John 11:1-44; catalyst for the plot to kill Jesus. After the Feast of Dedication (John 10:22, winter) and the stay beyond the Jordan (John 10:40), and shortly before the last Passover (John 11:55). Ussher, Annals §6427: AD 33.

events.name: Healing of Ten Lepers
events.description: Jesus heals ten lepers; only one (a Samaritan) returns to give thanks.
events.dateNotes: Luke 17:11-19; only in Luke. On the final journey to Jerusalem through Samaria and Galilee (Luke 17:11). Ussher, Annals §6418 lies under the heading AD 33 but before the Dedication paragraph (§6422, December); year kept at AD 33 and flagged approximate.

events.name: Healing of Blind Bartimaeus
events.description: As Jesus leaves Jericho on his last journey to Jerusalem, blind Bartimaeus son of Timaeus cries out to the Son of David and receives his sight (Mark 10:46-52). Matthew tells of two blind men (Matt 20:29-34) and Luke sets the healing as Jesus drew near to Jericho (Luke 18:35-43); most harmonies treat the three accounts as one incident.
events.dateNotes: Mark 10:46-52; Matthew 20:29-34; Luke 18:35-43. Days before the Triumphal Entry. Ussher, Annals §6432: AD 33.

events.name: Cursing of the Fig Tree
events.description: Jesus curses a barren fig tree and it withers.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 21:18-22; Mark 11:12-14, 20-25. The Monday of passion week. Ussher, Annals §6443: AD 33.

events.name: Healing of Malchus' Ear
events.description: Jesus heals the ear of the high priest's servant during his arrest.
events.dateNotes: Luke 22:49-51; John 18:10-11. Night of the arrest. Ussher, Annals §6463: AD 33.

events.name: Catch of 153 Fish
events.description: The risen Jesus directs a miraculous catch of 153 fish.
events.dateNotes: John 21:1-14; post-resurrection appearance at the Sea of Tiberias. Ussher, Annals §6492: AD 33.

events.name: Appearance to Mary Magdalene
events.description: Weeping at the empty tomb, Mary Magdalene mistook the risen Jesus for the gardener until he spoke her name, and she answered, Rabbouni. John records this first appearance, and Jesus' commission made her the first herald of the resurrection, honored in tradition as apostle to the apostles.
events.dateNotes: John 20:11-18; Mark 16:9-11. First post-resurrection appearance. Ussher, Annals §6486: AD 33.

events.name: Road to Emmaus
events.description: Two downcast disciples walking to Emmaus were joined by the risen Jesus, unrecognized, who opened Moses and all the prophets to show that the Messiah had to suffer and enter glory. Luke alone tells the story in full; their eyes were opened when he broke the bread, and their hearts burned within them.
events.dateNotes: Luke 24:13-35; Mark 16:12-13. On the day of resurrection. Ussher, Annals §6488: AD 33.

events.name: Appearance to the Disciples
events.description: On the evening of the resurrection, Jesus stood among his disciples behind locked doors, greeted them with peace, and showed them his hands and side. Luke notes that he ate broiled fish to prove he was no ghost, and John records him breathing on them the Holy Spirit and sending them as the Father sent him.
events.dateNotes: John 20:19-25; Luke 24:36-43. Thomas is absent. Ussher, Annals §6489: AD 33.

events.name: Appearance to Thomas
events.description: A week after the resurrection, Jesus invited doubting Thomas to touch his wounds, and Thomas answered with the gospels' most direct confession of Jesus' deity, calling him his Lord and his God. Found only in John, the scene ends with a blessing on all who believe without seeing.
events.dateNotes: John 20:26-29. A week after the resurrection. Ussher, Annals §6490: AD 33.

events.name: Restoration of Peter
events.description: Over a charcoal-fire breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias, the risen Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved him, mirroring Peter's three denials, and charged him to feed his sheep. John 21 records this restoration, which recommissioned the fallen disciple as shepherd of the early church.
events.dateNotes: John 21:15-19. Parallels Peter's three denials. Ussher, Annals §6492: AD 33.

events.name: Great Commission
events.description: On a mountain in Galilee, the risen Jesus claimed all authority in heaven and on earth and sent his disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptizing in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Matthew closes with this charge and the promise of Christ's presence to the end of the age.
events.dateNotes: Matthew 28:16-20; Mark 16:15-18. Foundation of Christian mission. Ussher, Annals §6491: AD 33.

people.role: One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)

events.name: Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem
events.description: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt while the crowds spread garments and branches and cry Hosanna to the Son of David, as in Zechariah 9:9. It opens the week of his passion.
events.dateNotes: The Sunday before the crucifixion (John 12:1, 12). Ussher gives 29 March AD 33 (AD 30 on the main alternative). Ussher, Annals §6438: AD 33.

events.name: Last Supper
events.description: On the night he was betrayed Jesus eats a final meal with the Twelve, washes their feet (John 13), gives them the bread and the cup as his body and his blood of the new covenant, and foretells Judas's betrayal and Peter's denial. Christians understand the Lord's Supper differently but all trace it to this meal.
events.dateNotes: The Synoptic Gospels call it the Passover meal (Luke 22:15); John places the crucifixion on the day of preparation (John 18:28; 19:14), a long-debated question of harmonisation. Ussher: Thursday 2 April AD 33. Ussher, Annals §6454: AD 33.

people.role: One of the twelve at the table
One of the twelve at the table; asked to see the Father (John 14:8)
One of the twelve at the table
One of the twelve at the table
One of the twelve at the table
One of the twelve at the table

events.name: Arrest and Trials of Jesus
events.description: After praying in Gethsemane, Jesus is arrested by a party guided by Judas and taken to Annas and Caiaphas and before the council, while Peter denies him three times. In the morning he is brought to Pilate, who sends him to Herod Antipas and then, after offering to release him instead of Barabbas, hands him over to be crucified.
events.dateNotes: From the night of the Last Supper to the morning of the crucifixion (Ussher: 3 April AD 33). Ussher, Annals §6467: AD 33.

events.name: Zacchaeus Meets Jesus in Jericho
events.description: As Jesus passes through Jericho on the way to Jerusalem, Zacchaeus, a wealthy chief tax collector too short to see over the crowd, climbs a sycamore tree. Jesus calls him down and stays at his house; Zacchaeus gives half his goods to the poor and repays fourfold. Jesus declares that salvation has come to the house.
events.dateNotes: Luke 19:1-10. Just before the Triumphal Entry (Luke 19:28). Ussher, Annals §6433: AD 33.

people.role: Chief tax collector who received Jesus
Called Zacchaeus down and stayed at his house

events.name: Gamaliel's Counsel before the Sanhedrin
events.description: After the apostles are arrested and freed by an angel, they are brought before the council and Peter answers that they must obey God rather than men. When the council wants to kill them, the Pharisee Gamaliel advises restraint: if the movement is of men it will come to nothing, but if of God no one can overthrow it. They beat the apostles and release them.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6516: AD 33, the year of Pentecost (Acts 5 follows Acts 2-4 closely). Earlier row put it in AD 34 by harmonisation.

people.role: Pharisee and teacher of the law who counselled restraint
Apostle who answered for the others

events.name: Philip Preaches in Samaria
events.description: Philip the evangelist proclaims Christ in Samaria; many believe and miracles accompany his preaching.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6526: AD 34, after the scattering that followed Stephen's death (Acts 8:1, 4-5).

events.name: Ethiopian Eunuch Baptized
events.description: Philip meets an Ethiopian official on the Gaza road, explains Isaiah 53, and baptizes him.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6532: AD 34, after Philip's work in Samaria (Acts 8:26-40).

events.name: Conversion of Paul
events.description: On the Damascus road, Saul of Tarsus, traveling to arrest followers of Jesus, was confronted by a blinding vision of the risen Christ. Acts recounts the event three times and Paul's letters confirm it, marking the turning point that made the church's fiercest persecutor its apostle to the Gentiles.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6533-6538: AD 35, the year after the dispersion (Acts 8:1; 9:1-19). Scripture's intervals: Paul went up to Jerusalem "after three years" (Gal 1:18; Ussher AD 37, 6587) and again "fourteen years after" (Gal 2:1; Ussher AD 52, 6753), so 17 years from conversion to the council on inclusive counting. Scholars commonly give AD 33-36.

events.name: Peter Raises Tabitha in Joppa
events.description: Peter raises the disciple Tabitha (Dorcas) from the dead in Joppa.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6599-6600: AD 38, in Peter's tour of the churches that had rest (Acts 9:31-43); before Cornelius (AD 40).

events.name: Peter and Cornelius in Caesarea
events.description: Guided by paired visions, Peter entered the house of Cornelius, a centurion of the Italian Cohort in Caesarea, and preached Christ to Gentiles. When the Holy Spirit fell on the hearers before baptism, this Gentile Pentecost convinced the Jerusalem church that God shows no partiality, opening the door to the nations.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6657-6659: AD 40, in the first year of Claudius (Acts 10-11). Scripture gives no year.

events.name: Church Established in Antioch
events.description: Believers are first called Christians in Antioch as Barnabas and Saul teach the church for a year.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6667: AD 43, when Barnabas brought Saul to Antioch and they taught "a whole year" (Acts 11:26); the gospel first came to Greeks there about AD 40 (6664, Acts 11:19-21).

people.role: Prophet who came to Antioch and foretold the famine (Acts 11:27-28)

events.name: James Killed and Peter Imprisoned by Agrippa I
events.description: Herod Agrippa I has James the brother of John killed with the sword and, seeing that it pleased the people, arrests Peter during the days of unleavened bread. An angel frees Peter, who goes to the house of Mary the mother of John Mark. Soon afterwards Agrippa is struck down at Caesarea and dies.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6674-6679: AD 44, at Passover shortly before Agrippa I died at Caesarea (Acts 12:2-3, 23; Josephus Ant. 19.343-352).

events.name: Famine Relief Sent from Antioch to Judea
events.description: The prophet Agabus comes to Antioch and foretells a great famine, which comes in the reign of Claudius. The disciples there decide each according to his means to send relief to the believers in Judea, and Barnabas and Saul carry the gift to the elders at Jerusalem.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6668, 6673: Agabus foretells the famine in AD 43; the gift is sent and carried in AD 44, the year of Agrippa I's death (Acts 11:27-30; 12:25). Ussher also notes a famine in Claudius's second year (AD 41, 6666) and an eleventh-year famine. Earlier row had AD 46.

people.role: Emperor in whose reign the famine came
Carried the relief to Jerusalem (as Saul)

events.name: Paul's First Missionary Journey
events.description: Barnabas and Saul, sent out from Antioch by the Holy Spirit (Acts 13:2-3), travel through Cyprus and southern Galatia (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe) and return to Antioch.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6691-6710: AD 45, after the famine visit of AD 44 (Acts 12:25; 13:1-3); they then stayed at Antioch "a long time" (Acts 14:28; 6712). Earlier row had AD 47-49 (a common modern estimate).

events.name: Barnabas and Saul in Cyprus
events.description: Paul blinds the sorcerer Bar-Jesus on Cyprus; the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus believes.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6692: AD 45, first stop of the first journey (Acts 13:4-12).

events.name: Paul Preaches in Pisidian Antioch
events.description: Paul preaches in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch; many believe but Jews stir up opposition and drive the missionaries out.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6698-6699: AD 45 (Acts 13:14-52).

events.name: Iconium — Belief and Opposition
events.description: Paul and Barnabas preach in Iconium; the city divides; they flee before a planned stoning.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6700-6701: AD 45 (Acts 14:1-7).

events.name: Lystra — Healing and Stoning
events.description: Paul heals a man lame from birth in Lystra; the crowd hails them as gods, then stones Paul and leaves him for dead.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6702-6705: AD 45 (Acts 14:8-20). Ussher also thinks Paul's rapture to the third heaven (2 Cor 12:2-4, "fourteen years" before 2 Corinthians) may belong here (6703).

events.name: Derbe — Many Disciples
events.description: Paul and Barnabas make many disciples in Derbe and begin the return journey strengthening the new churches.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6706: AD 45 (Acts 14:20-21).

events.name: James Written
events.description: James, brother of Jesus, writes the earliest NT epistle from Jerusalem — practical wisdom on faith and works, addressed to Jewish Christians scattered abroad.
events.dateNotes: Estimate, consistent with Scripture and Ussher: written before the council of AD 52 and by AD 63, when James was martyred (Ussher 6886). Often dated AD 45-49; some date it later (AD 60s).

events.name: Council of Jerusalem
events.description: Apostles and elders gathered to decide whether Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. After Peter testified that Jews and Gentiles alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus (Acts 15:11) and James gave his judgment, the council freed Gentile believers from circumcision and asked them to abstain from food offered to idols, blood, things strangled and sexual immorality (Acts 15:20, 29).
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6753-6757: AD 52, "fourteen years after" Paul's first Jerusalem visit of AD 37 (Gal 1:18; 2:1), Gal 2 being identified with Acts 15. Earlier row had AD 49; modern scholars range AD 48-50, and some identify Gal 2:1 with the famine visit of Acts 11:30.

people.role: Went up to Jerusalem with Paul and Barnabas; not compelled to be circumcised (Gal 2:1-3)

events.name: Paul's Second Missionary Journey
events.description: Paul brings the gospel to Greece.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6780-6819: begins AD 53, after the council (AD 52) and a stay at Antioch (Acts 15:35-36); Corinth AD 54-56 (Acts 18:11); return to Caesarea, Jerusalem and Antioch AD 56 (Acts 18:22). Earlier row had AD 50-52.

events.name: Macedonian Vision at Troas
events.description: Paul receives a vision at Troas: "Come over to Macedonia and help us." The gospel crosses into Europe.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6783-6784: AD 53 (Acts 16:8-10).

events.name: Lydia Converted in Philippi
events.description: Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, becomes the first European convert; Paul and Silas are imprisoned and the jailer is converted.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6785-6787: AD 53 (Acts 16:11-40).

events.name: Paul in Thessalonica
events.description: Paul reasons in the synagogue at Thessalonica for three Sabbaths; opponents accuse the missionaries of "turning the world upside down."
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6788-6790: AD 53 (Acts 17:1-9; three Sabbath days, Acts 17:2).

events.name: Noble-Minded Bereans
events.description: The Bereans receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily to verify Paul's message.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6791: AD 53, after Thessalonica (Acts 17:10-15).

events.name: 1 Thessalonians Written
events.description: Paul writes from Corinth, with Silvanus and Timothy (1 Thess 1:1; 3:6), to encourage the young Thessalonian church, with teaching on the return of Christ. It is the earliest of Paul's letters in this chronology.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6803: AD 54, after Timothy returned from Macedonia to Corinth (1 Thess 3:6; Acts 18:5). Earlier row had AD 51.

events.name: Paul on the Areopagus in Athens
events.description: Paul addresses the philosophers of Athens on Mars Hill, proclaiming the "Unknown God" and the resurrection.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6793-6794: AD 54, while Paul waited at Athens for Silas and Timothy (Acts 17:16-34).

events.name: Paul in Corinth — 18 Months
events.description: Paul stays 18 months with Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth; the proconsul Gallio dismisses charges against him.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6798-6818: Paul reaches Corinth in AD 54, stays "a year and six months" (Acts 18:11) with Gallio's judgment in late AD 54 (6815, Acts 18:12-17), and sails in AD 56. The Gallio inscription at Delphi is commonly dated AD 51-52, which would move Paul's stay to c. AD 50-52.

events.name: Claudius Expels the Jews from Rome
events.description: The emperor Claudius orders all Jews to leave Rome. Among those who go is the couple Aquila and Priscilla, who settle in Corinth and there welcome Paul. The edict is probably tied to disturbances in the Jewish community, which the Roman historian Suetonius links to a certain "Chrestus".
events.dateNotes: Scripture: Aquila and Priscilla were "lately come from Italy" when Paul reached Corinth (Acts 18:2). Ussher, Annals 6792, 6798: places the expulsion immediately before Paul's arrival in AD 54 (Claudius died October AD 54); he does not date the decree separately. Orosius gives AD 49, the common modern date.

events.name: 2 Thessalonians Written
events.description: Paul writes a follow-up to Thessalonica, correcting misunderstandings about the Day of the Lord and urging believers to continue working.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6803: written "later" than 1 Thessalonians with Silvanus and Timothy still with Paul (2 Thess 1:1), so during the Corinth stay of AD 54-56. AD 55 is an estimate within that span.

events.name: Matthew Written
events.description: The Gospel of Matthew is composed, presenting Jesus as the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecy, structured around five major discourses.
events.dateNotes: Estimate: Ussher does not date it. Early tradition (Irenaeus, Origen) puts Matthew first, c. AD 50-60; most modern scholars place it after Mark, c. AD 70-90.

events.name: Mark Written
events.description: Mark composes a fast-paced account of Jesus' ministry. Early church tradition (Papias, Irenaeus) says it records Peter's preaching; most modern scholars regard it as the earliest Gospel, while the church fathers generally placed Matthew first.
events.dateNotes: Estimate: Ussher does not date the Gospel, and records that Mark died at Alexandria in Nero's 8th year (Jerome; Annals 6864), though 2 Tim 4:11 has Mark alive in AD 66. AD 55 is a tradition-based estimate; Irenaeus places Mark after the deaths of Peter and Paul, Clement of Alexandria during Peter's life. Modern range AD 50-70.

events.name: Paul's Third Missionary Journey
events.description: Paul strengthens churches in Asia Minor and Greece.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6819-6848: begins AD 56 after the stay at Antioch (Acts 18:22-23); Ephesus AD 57-59 (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31); Macedonia and three months in Greece AD 60 (Acts 20:2-3); Jerusalem by Pentecost AD 60 (Acts 20:16). Earlier row had AD 54-58.

events.name: Paul in Ephesus — 2 Years
events.description: Paul teaches in Ephesus for over two years with extraordinary miracles; new believers burn their occult scrolls; Demetrius the silversmith starts a riot.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6822-6838: Paul reaches Ephesus in AD 57 and leaves in AD 59; Acts 19:10 gives two years in the school of Tyrannus (Acts 20:31 "three years" counts the whole stay).

events.name: Galatians Written
events.description: Paul writes to the Galatian churches defending justification by faith alone against Judaizers who insisted Gentile converts must follow the Mosaic Law.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6830: AD 58, soon after Paul left the Galatians (Acts 18:23); Gal 2:1-10 recounts the Jerusalem visit Ussher identifies with the council of AD 52, so the letter must be later. Earlier row had AD 49 on the South Galatian theory; North Galatian theory c. AD 53-55.

events.name: 1 Corinthians Written
events.description: Paul writes from Ephesus to the divided Corinthian church, addressing disputes, immorality, spiritual gifts, and the resurrection — including the great love chapter (ch. 13).
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6835: AD 59, written from Ephesus ("I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost", 1 Cor 16:8). Earlier row had AD 57.

people.role: Named in the letter; Paul urged him to visit Corinth (1 Cor 16:12)

events.name: 2 Corinthians Written
events.description: Paul writes his most personal letter from Macedonia, defending his apostleship and describing his sufferings — "when I am weak, then I am strong."
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6841: AD 60, from Macedonia after Titus's report (2 Cor 2:12-13; 7:5-7). Scripture: 2 Cor 12:2 looks back "fourteen years" to an experience Ussher places in AD 45 (6703). Earlier row had AD 57.

events.name: Romans Written
events.description: Paul writes his theological masterpiece from Corinth to the Roman church — the fullest exposition of justification by faith, the role of the Law, and God's plan for Jews and Gentiles.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6843: AD 60, from Corinth during the three months in Greece (Acts 20:2-3; Rom 15:25-26; 16:1, 23). Earlier row had AD 57.

events.name: Luke Written
events.description: Luke the physician composes his orderly Gospel account, addressed to Theophilus — the most detailed account of Jesus' birth and parables unique to Luke.
events.dateNotes: Estimate: Luke wrote before Acts (Acts 1:1) and was with Paul at Caesarea in AD 60-62 (Acts 27:1; Ussher 6784, 6855-6873). Traditional range AD 58-63.

events.name: Farewell to Ephesian Elders at Miletus
events.description: Paul calls the Ephesian elders to Miletus for an emotional farewell: "I have not coveted anyone's silver or gold."
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6848: spring AD 60, as Paul hurried to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (Acts 20:16). Earlier row had AD 58.

events.name: Paul Arrested in Jerusalem
events.description: Paul is seized in the temple, beaten by the crowd, and transferred to Roman custody under the tribune Claudius Lysias.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6851-6853: Pentecost AD 60 (Acts 21:17-23:10). Earlier row had AD 58 (many scholars AD 57).

events.name: Paul's Trial before Felix and Festus
events.description: Paul is held in Caesarea two years under Felix (Acts 24:27), then stands before his successor Festus; he defends himself before Agrippa II and Bernice and appeals to Caesar.
events.dateNotes: Scripture: two years under Felix, then Festus (Acts 24:27). Ussher, Annals 6855-6869: Paul is in Caesarea AD 60-62; Festus arrives AD 62 (6868) and Agrippa II hears Paul (Acts 25-26). Earlier row had AD 58-60.

events.name: Storm and Fair Havens of Crete
events.description: Paul warns against sailing late in the season; a violent northeaster batters the ship for 14 days as it drifts toward Malta.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6873-6874: autumn AD 62, after the Day of Atonement fast (Acts 27:9). Earlier row had AD 60.

events.name: Shipwreck on Malta
events.description: All 276 aboard reach shore safely; Paul is bitten by a viper but unharmed and heals the sick on the island for three months.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6874-6877: shipwreck late AD 62; three months on Malta (Acts 28:11) until early AD 63. Earlier row had AD 60.

events.name: Landing at Puteoli
events.description: Paul and his companions land at the Italian port of Puteoli and stay seven days with believers there.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6877-6878: spring AD 63, after the winter on Malta (Acts 28:11-14). Earlier row had AD 61.

events.name: Paul Arrives in Rome
events.description: After appealing to Caesar, surviving shipwreck at Malta, Paul reached Rome under guard and spent two years in rented lodging, welcoming all and preaching the kingdom unhindered. Acts closes with the gospel proclaimed in the empire's capital, and tradition places several prison epistles in this period.
events.dateNotes: Scripture: "two whole years" in his own hired house (Acts 28:30). Ussher, Annals 6878, 6915: arrival AD 63, release AD 65. Earlier row had AD 61-63.

events.name: Martyrdom of James, Brother of Jesus
events.description: James, leader of the Jerusalem church, is condemned by the high priest Ananus and stoned at Jerusalem while Judea is without a Roman governor. Josephus records the event, and the second-century writer Hegesippus (quoted by Eusebius) gives a fuller account. Scripture does not record it.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6885-6887: AD 63, after the death of Festus and before Albinus arrived (Josephus Ant. 20.197-203). Many modern scholars date this AD 62.

events.name: Ephesians Written
events.description: Paul writes from Roman imprisonment on the cosmic scope of God's plan — the church as the body of Christ, spiritual blessings, and the armor of God.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6910-6912: AD 64, during the two years in Rome (Acts 28:30; AD 63-65), carried by Tychicus (Eph 6:21). Earlier row had AD 62; some place the Prison Epistles at Caesarea or Ephesus.

events.name: Colossians Written
events.description: Paul writes from prison to Colossae affirming Christ's supremacy over all creation and warning against false philosophy — "in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily."
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6909: AD 64, sent with Onesimus and Tychicus (Col 4:7-9) during the Roman imprisonment of AD 63-65. Earlier row had AD 62.

events.name: Philemon Written
events.description: Paul writes a brief personal letter from prison urging Philemon to receive his runaway slave Onesimus back as a brother in Christ — a window into early Christian social ethics.
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6906, 6909: AD 64, sent with Onesimus (Phlm 10-12) during the Roman imprisonment of AD 63-65. Earlier row had AD 62.

people.role: Runaway slave Paul sends back with the letter

events.name: Philippians Written
events.description: Paul writes his letter of joy from prison to his most supportive church — including the great Christ-hymn (2:5-11) and "I can do all things through him who strengthens me."
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6905, 6908: AD 64, sent by Epaphroditus during the Roman imprisonment of AD 63-65 (Phil 2:25; 4:18). Earlier row had AD 62-63.

events.name: 1 Peter Written
events.description: Peter writes from Rome (called "Babylon") to persecuted Christians scattered across Asia Minor, encouraging them to stand firm — "you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood."
events.dateNotes: Estimate: Ussher does not date it. Written from Rome (1 Pet 5:13, "Babylon") before 2 Peter (AD 66; 2 Pet 3:1), and before or about the persecution of AD 64. Range AD 62-64.

events.name: Hebrews Written
events.description: An unknown author writes this sophisticated argument for Christ's superiority over angels, Moses, and the Levitical priesthood — "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever."
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6907, 6913: AD 64, soon after Timothy's release (Heb 13:23) with greetings from "they of Italy" (Heb 13:24); Ussher takes Paul as author. Authorship is not stated in the text and was long debated. Earlier row had AD 67.

events.name: Great Fire of Rome and Nero's Persecution
events.description: In July AD 64 a fire destroys much of Rome. Rumour blames Nero, who fastens the guilt on the Christians and has many of them put to death with great cruelty (Tacitus). It is the first known Roman state violence against Christians.
events.dateNotes: Tacitus, Annals 15.38-44, dates the fire to July AD 64.

events.name: Acts Written
events.description: Luke composes Acts as the sequel to his Gospel, tracing the spread of the church from Jerusalem to Rome — ending abruptly with Paul under house arrest.
events.dateNotes: Scripture: Acts ends after Paul's "two whole years" in Rome (Acts 28:30), which Ussher dates AD 63-65 (6878, 6915), so the book is finished about AD 65. Estimate: the date of writing is not given. Earlier row had AD 63; many scholars date Acts AD 80-90.

events.name: 1 Timothy Written
events.description: Paul writes to his young protégé Timothy at Ephesus with instructions on church leadership, false teaching, and godly conduct — "fight the good fight of the faith."
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6923-6924: AD 65, after Paul's release (6915) and journey from Ephesus to Macedonia (1 Tim 1:3). Assumes release after Acts 28:30 (early tradition: 1 Clement 5). Earlier row had AD 64.

events.name: Titus Written
events.description: Paul writes to Titus on Crete with instructions for appointing elders and promoting sound doctrine — "the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people."
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6918, 6925: AD 65, written after Paul left Titus in Crete (Titus 1:5) and planned to winter at Nicopolis (Titus 3:12). Assumes release after Acts 28:30. Earlier row had AD 64.

events.name: Jude Written
events.description: Jude, brother of Jesus, writes a brief, urgent letter warning against false teachers who have infiltrated the church — "contend for the faith once delivered to the saints."
events.dateNotes: Estimate: Ussher does not date it. Jude was a brother of James (Jude 1), who died in AD 63; 2 Peter (AD 66) appears to draw on it, so c. AD 65. Modern range AD 65-80, and some reverse the dependence.

events.name: 2 Timothy Written
events.description: Paul writes his final letter from a Roman dungeon to Timothy — a deeply personal farewell: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith."
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6937, 6939: AD 66, second Roman imprisonment, Paul expecting death (2 Tim 4:6-8). Earlier row had AD 67; death under Nero is tradition (1 Clement 5; Ussher AD 67, 6949).

events.name: 2 Peter Written
events.description: Peter writes his final letter shortly before his martyrdom, warning against false teachers and affirming the certainty of Christ's return — "with the Lord one day is as a thousand years."
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6937-6938: AD 66, shortly before Peter's death (2 Pet 1:14); written after a first letter (2 Pet 3:1). Earlier row had AD 67.

events.name: Martyrdom of Peter and Paul
events.description: Early church tradition holds that Peter and Paul were both put to death at Rome under Nero, Paul by the sword and Peter by crucifixion (1 Clement 5; Eusebius). Scripture does not record either death, though Jesus foretells Peter's (John 21:18-19) and Paul anticipates his own (2 Tim 4:6-8).
events.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6949: Paul beheaded at Rome on 29 June AD 67, Peter martyred at the same time (Dionysius of Corinth; Origen), both before Nero's death in June AD 68. Scripture does not record either death. Eusebius's Chronicle gives AD 67/68; some link it to the AD 64 persecution.

events.name: Destruction of Jerusalem
events.description: Roman legions under Titus crushed the Jewish revolt, burning the city and demolishing the Second Temple. The catastrophe ended sacrificial worship, scattered the Jewish people, and echoed Jesus' warning that no stone would be left on another; the Arch of Titus in Rome still depicts the looted menorah.
events.dateNotes: Standard history (the Annals end at AD 73): Josephus, War 6; the Temple burned in the month of Av (August) AD 70. Ussher agrees (Annals 6968ff.); Masada fell AD 73 (6992).

people.role: Emperor who sent his son to finish the war

events.name: John Written
events.description: The apostle John composes his Gospel in Ephesus — a theological masterpiece opening with "In the beginning was the Word," presenting Jesus as the divine Son of God.
events.dateNotes: Estimate (tradition): Irenaeus and Eusebius place John at Ephesus into the 80s-90s. Range AD 85-95.

events.name: 1 John Written
events.description: John writes his first epistle from Ephesus, countering early Gnostic-like heresies and declaring that "God is light" and "God is love."
events.dateNotes: Estimate (tradition): AD 85-95, Ephesus.

events.name: 2 John Written
events.description: John writes a brief letter to "the elect lady and her children" — a local church — warning against false teachers who deny Christ came in the flesh.
events.dateNotes: Estimate (tradition): AD 85-95, Ephesus.

events.name: 3 John Written
events.description: John writes to Gaius commending his hospitality to traveling missionaries and rebuking Diotrephes, who "likes to put himself first."
events.dateNotes: Estimate (tradition): AD 85-95, Ephesus.

events.name: John Writes Revelation
events.description: Exiled on the rocky island of Patmos, John received sweeping visions of the risen Christ, letters for seven churches of Asia Minor, and the final triumph of the Lamb. Written to believers under Roman pressure, it closes the canon with the promise of a new heaven and new earth; Irenaeus placed it late in Domitian's reign.
events.dateNotes: Standard history: Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3) places the vision late in Domitian's reign (81-96), c. AD 95; Ussher's Annals do not reach it. Early date (c. AD 65, Nero) is the main alternative.

events.name: Death of John
events.description: According to early tradition (Irenaeus, Eusebius), John lived at Ephesus into the reign of Trajan (from AD 98) and died there, the last of the Twelve; his death is taken to close the Apostolic Age. Scripture records nothing about it (John 21:23 only corrects a rumour that he would not die).
events.dateNotes: Tradition (Irenaeus, Eusebius): died at Ephesus under Trajan (from AD 98), c. AD 98-100. Estimate; not in Scripture or the Annals.

events.name: Martyrdom of Ignatius of Antioch
events.description: Bishop Ignatius of Antioch is taken to Rome and executed under Trajan; his seven letters on church order, the Eucharist and martyrdom are among the earliest post-apostolic writings.
events.dateNotes: Traditional date c. 108 (Eusebius, Church History III.36, under Trajan, 98-117); modern estimates range from c. 107 to c. 117.

events.name: Martyrdom of Polycarp
events.description: Bishop Polycarp of Smyrna is put to death in the stadium at Smyrna, saying "Eighty-six years I have served Him, and He never did me any injury." In the earliest account the flames did not consume him and he was finally stabbed.
events.dateNotes: 22/23 February, 155 or 156 (standard modern view); Eusebius's Chronicle implies c. 166-167, which most scholars reject.

events.name: Irenaeus Writes Against Heresies
events.description: Irenaeus of Lyon writes Against Heresies (the Greek original is largely lost; a complete Latin translation survives), refuting Gnostic teaching and appealing to Scripture, the rule of faith and the succession of bishops from the apostles.
events.dateNotes: Written in Greek, c. 175-185, while Irenaeus was bishop of Lyon (Book III mentions Eleutherus as pope, 174-189).

events.name: Tertullian Writes the Apology
events.description: Tertullian of Carthage addresses the Roman governors in defence of Christians, arguing that they are loyal subjects and that persecution is unjust. He is the first major Christian author to write in Latin, and the work shows the church in North Africa.
events.dateNotes: Apologeticus is usually dated to 197.

events.name: Origen Opens Catechetical School
events.description: Origen, at about age 18, becomes head of the catechetical school in Alexandria, beginning a career of biblical scholarship and allegorical interpretation.
events.dateNotes: Eusebius, Church History VI.3, gives his age as 18 under Bishop Demetrius; c. 203.

events.name: Conversion of Armenia
events.description: According to Armenian tradition, Gregory the Illuminator converts King Tiridates III, making Armenia the first state to adopt Christianity officially. The Armenian Apostolic Church remains one of the oldest national churches.
events.dateNotes: Traditional date 301; some scholars prefer c. 314.

people.role: Baptised the king and led the church

events.name: Diocletian Persecution Begins
events.description: Emperor Diocletian and his co-emperors issue edicts ordering churches destroyed, scriptures burned and clergy imprisoned: the most severe empire-wide persecution, though enforcement varied widely from region to region.
events.dateNotes: Eusebius, Church History VIII; Diocletian issued edicts in 303-304.

events.name: Constantine Proclaimed Emperor at York
events.description: When Constantius I dies at York in July 306, his troops proclaim his son Constantine emperor. After years of civil war this begins his rise to sole rule and the end of imperial persecution.
events.dateNotes: Constantius died 25 July 306; Constantine was acclaimed that day.

people.role: Dying emperor; his death opens the succession

events.name: Edict of Milan
events.description: In 313 the emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed to extend religious toleration to Christians and other cults and to restore confiscated church property, building on Galerius's edict of toleration (311). Christianity became a legally protected faith, though not yet the state religion.
events.dateNotes: Agreement reached at Milan in early 313; the text survives as Licinius's rescript issued at Nicomedia in June 313 (Lactantius, De Mortibus Persecutorum 48; Eusebius, Church History X.5). Galerius had already granted toleration in 311.

events.name: Council of Nicaea
events.description: Constantine convened bishops from across the empire at Nicaea to settle the Arian controversy over the Son's divinity. The council confessed Christ as homoousios, of one being with the Father; the Nicene Creed in use today is the form expanded at Constantinople in 381. Tradition numbers the assembled bishops at 318.
events.dateNotes: First Ecumenical Council, convened by Constantine at Nicaea, May-June 325.

events.name: Helena Journeys to the Holy Land
events.description: Helena, mother of Constantine, travels to Jerusalem and Palestine and supports church building at sites tied to the life of Christ. Later tradition says she found the True Cross; this is a legend first recorded decades afterward, not something Eusebius reports. Constantines churches at the Holy Sepulchre and Bethlehem belong to the same programme.
events.dateNotes: Eusebius dates the visit shortly before her death c. 330; 326-328 in modern accounts. The True Cross story is later tradition.

people.role: Imperial sponsor of the building programme

events.name: Conversion of the Kingdom of Aksum (Ethiopia)
events.description: Under King Ezana, Aksum embraces Christianity through the missionary Frumentius, consecrated first bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church traces its origin here.
events.dateNotes: c. 330-340; Rufinus (Church History I.9) and Ezana's inscriptions and coins.

events.name: Athanasius Lists the 27 NT Books
events.description: In his thirty-ninth Festal Letter from Alexandria, Bishop Athanasius listed exactly the twenty-seven books of today's New Testament, the earliest surviving list to match it precisely. Calling them the springs of salvation, he distinguished canonical Scripture from disputed and spurious writings.
events.dateNotes: Athanasius, 39th Festal Letter (367 AD).

events.name: Council of Constantinople
events.description: The Second Ecumenical Council, called by Theodosius I, reaffirms Nicaea against Arian and Macedonian views and confesses the deity of the Holy Spirit. The creed now recited as the Nicene Creed (the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed) is linked to this council.
events.dateNotes: May-July 381.

people.role: Bishop who led the council at first

events.name: Jerome Translates the Latin Bible (the Vulgate)
events.description: Beginning at the request of Pope Damasus in Rome (382) and continuing in his monastery at Bethlehem, Jerome revised the Latin Gospels and Psalms and translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew text he called the hebraica veritas rather than from the Greek Septuagint. The resulting Vulgate became the standard Bible of Western Christendom for about a thousand years.
events.dateNotes: Begun 382 under Damasus; the Old Testament translation from Hebrew was finished c. 405. The name 'Vulgate' and the final composition of the book came later.

events.name: Augustines Conversion and Baptism
events.description: In a garden at Milan in 386, Augustine hears a childs voice say take up and read, opens Romans 13, and is converted. With his son Adeodatus he is baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387. He describes it in his Confessions; his mother Monica died soon after, on the way back to Africa.
events.dateNotes: Confessions Books 8-9. Conversion August 386; baptism Easter 24-25 April 387.

events.name: Council of Carthage Affirms the Biblical Canon
events.description: A synod of North African bishops, in which Augustine took part, affirmed a list of Scripture that included the twenty-seven New Testament books and an Old Testament that included the books Protestants call the Apocrypha. Following the earlier synod of Hippo (393), it was a regional statement that later received wider authority in the West; the Eastern churches and the Reformers did not adopt it unchanged.
events.dateNotes: Council of Carthage, 397 AD (the list is also reaffirmed at Carthage in 419).

events.name: John Chrysostom Preaches at Constantinople
events.description: Appointed archbishop of Constantinople in 398, John gains the name Chrysostom (golden-mouthed) for preaching that presses wealth, justice and care for the poor. His criticism of the court brings him exile in 403 and a final banishment in 404. He died in exile in 407.
events.dateNotes: Consecrated 26 February 398; exiled finally June 404; died 14 September 407.

events.name: Council of Ephesus
events.description: The Third Ecumenical Council, meeting June-July 431, condemns Nestorius, affirms that Mary may be called Theotokos (God-bearer), and upholds the unity of Christ's person. The Church of the East did not accept it.
events.dateNotes: Opened 22 June 431.

events.name: Patricks Mission to Ireland
events.description: Patrick, a Briton once taken to Ireland as a slave, returns as a missionary bishop and plants churches there. His own Confession is the main source. Tradition puts his arrival in 432 and the founding of Armagh a little later; many modern scholars place his work later in the fifth century.
events.dateNotes: Traditional date 432 from later Irish annals; the date is disputed.

events.name: Council of Chalcedon
events.description: Bishops meeting at Chalcedon defined that Christ is one person in two natures, fully God and fully man, without confusion or separation. Guided by Pope Leo's Tome against Eutyches' teaching, the definition became the standard of Christology for the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and most Protestant churches; the Oriental Orthodox churches did not accept it, and the division has lasted.
events.dateNotes: Fourth Ecumenical Council, Chalcedon (451 AD).

people.role: Pope whose Tome shaped the definition

events.name: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
events.description: Romulus Augustulus, traditionally counted as the last Western Roman emperor, is deposed by Odoacer. The church, already organised under bishops across the former provinces, became a main carrier of continuity in a fragmented West.
events.dateNotes: Traditional date: 476 AD.

events.name: Benedict Writes His Rule
events.description: Benedict of Nursia writes his Rule for monks, which became the standard foundation of Western monastic life and helped preserve learning in the early Middle Ages. The later motto "ora et labora" (pray and work) sums up its spirit.
events.dateNotes: Rule of St. Benedict, traditionally c. 530 at Monte Cassino; some scholars date it to c. 540s. It draws on the earlier anonymous Rule of the Master.

events.name: Gregory the Great Sends Augustine to England
events.description: Pope Gregory I sends the monk Augustine and about forty companions to Kent. King Aethelberht lets them preach in Canterbury, and the mission founds the English churchs see there.
events.dateNotes: Landing in Kent 597 (Bede, Ecclesiastical History I).

events.name: Rise of Islam and Muslim Conquests
events.description: After Muhammad's death (632), Muslim armies conquer Syria, Egypt and North Africa, most of them long Christian lands, and the Sasanian Persian Empire, home to the Church of the East, within about a century, permanently altering the geography of Christianity.
events.dateNotes: Rapid expansion of the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphates, 632–750 AD.

people.role: Founder of Islam; the conquests followed his death

events.name: Alopen Brings Christianity to China
events.description: The Church of the East missionary Alopen reaches Chang'an and is received by Emperor Taizong. The Xi'an Stele (781) records the early Christian presence in Tang China.
events.dateNotes: Arrival 635 per the Xi'an Stele (781).

events.name: Synod of Whitby
events.description: King Oswiu of Northumbria decides in favor of the Roman method of dating Easter and the Roman tonsure over the Ionan (Celtic) customs, aligning the Northumbrian church with Rome.
events.dateNotes: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People, III.25.

people.role: Abbess and host of the synod

events.name: Second Council of Nicaea
events.description: The Seventh Ecumenical Council restores the veneration of icons after the iconoclast controversy, distinguishing veneration from the worship due to God alone. It is the last council accepted by both Catholic and Orthodox churches as ecumenical.
events.dateNotes: September-October 787.

events.name: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.description: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor of the Romans on Christmas Day, 800, reviving the imperial title in the West; the Byzantine empire contested it. The title 'Holy Roman Emperor' came later.
events.dateNotes: December 25, 800 AD; recorded by Einhard and the Royal Frankish Annals.

events.name: Cyril and Methodius Mission to Moravia
events.description: The Byzantine brothers Cyril and Methodius reach Great Moravia, creating the Glagolitic script and translating Scripture and liturgy into Slavic, laying the foundation for Slavic Christianity.
events.dateNotes: Arrival 863; Cyril died 869, Methodius 885.

events.name: Great Schism: East-West Split
events.description: In July 1054 Cardinal Humbert, legate of Pope Leo IX (who had died that April), laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and Patriarch Michael Cerularius and his synod responded in kind. The episode became the conventional date for the division of Christendom into a Roman Catholic West and an Orthodox East, though the estrangement over papal authority, the filioque clause and diverging customs was gradual and long in the making.
events.dateNotes: In July 1054 Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius excommunicated one another, an episode that became the conventional date for the split; the estrangement was gradual and the mutual anathemas of 1054 were lifted in 1965.

people.role: Papal legate who delivered the excommunication
Pope who sent the legates; died before they acted

events.name: Council of Clermont — First Crusade Called
events.description: Pope Urban II calls on Christians to aid the Byzantine Empire and recover Jerusalem; the exact wording of the speech is known only from later accounts. The First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099, beginning two centuries of Crusading warfare.
events.dateNotes: Pope Urban II's speech at the Council of Clermont, November 1095.

people.role: Pope who called for the crusade

events.name: Francis of Assisi Founds the Franciscans
events.description: Francis renounces his wealthy life and founds the Order of Friars Minor, preaching radical poverty, simplicity, and care for the poor.
events.dateNotes: Francis received papal approval in 1209/1210.

events.name: Thomas Aquinas Writes the Summa Theologiae
events.description: Aquinas works on his Summa Theologiae from about 1265 until he stops writing in December 1273, leaving the third part unfinished at his death in 1274. It became one of the most influential works of Christian theology, setting out faith and reason in a single systematic plan.
events.dateNotes: Begun c. 1265; Aquinas ceased writing in December 1273 and died 7 March 1274, leaving the work incomplete.

events.name: The Wycliffe Bible Appears in English
events.description: The first complete Bible in English, translated from the Latin Vulgate, appears in the Wycliffe circle: an Early Version c. 1382, largely by Nicholas Hereford, and a smoother Later Version c. 1388-1395 by John Purvey and others. Spread in hand-copied manuscripts by his Lollard followers, it survives in nearly 250 copies; Wycliffe himself was condemned after death.
events.dateNotes: Early Version c. 1382 (largely Nicholas Hereford); Later Version c. 1388-1395 (John Purvey and others). Wycliffe's personal share is uncertain.

events.name: Jan Hus Martyred
events.description: Czech reformer Jan Hus is condemned as a heretic and burned at the stake at the Council of Constance, which judged his teaching on the church and papal authority heretical; he had also preached in Czech.
events.dateNotes: July 6, 1415, at the Council of Constance.

events.name: Fall of Constantinople
events.description: On 29 May 1453 Ottoman forces under Mehmed II take Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire and placing the Ecumenical Patriarchate under Ottoman rule.

people.role: Ottoman sultan who took the city

events.name: Gutenberg Prints the Bible
events.description: In Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg used movable metal type to print the Latin Vulgate in a run of perhaps 180 copies on paper and vellum, of which about 49 survive. The 42-line Bible was the first major book printed with movable type in Europe, and the press it launched would carry Scripture and reform across the continent.
events.dateNotes: Gutenberg Bible printed c. 1454-1455 in Mainz; copies were on sale by March 1455.

events.name: Martin Luther Posts the 95 Theses
events.description: Martin Luther challenged the sale of indulgences with ninety-five theses for academic debate, which he sent to Archbishop Albert of Mainz; that he also posted them on the Wittenberg castle church door is traditional. Printers spread them across Germany within weeks, and they became the opening of the Reformation.
events.dateNotes: 31 October 1517: Luther sent the Theses to Archbishop Albert of Mainz on this date, which is certain. Whether he also nailed them to the Castle Church door is traditional and doubted by some historians.

events.name: Diet of Worms
events.description: Summoned before Emperor Charles V, Martin Luther refused to recant his writings, declaring his conscience captive to the Word of God. Outlawed by the Edict of Worms (May 1521), he was sheltered at Wartburg Castle, where he translated the New Testament into German from the Greek.

events.name: Luther Marries Katharina von Bora
events.description: A former nun who left her convent in 1523, Katharina marries Martin Luther at Wittenberg on 13 June 1525. Their household becomes the model of the Protestant parsonage, and she manages its finances and the Black Cloister.

events.name: Tyndale's New Testament Published
events.description: William Tyndale published the first printed English New Testament, translated directly from Erasmus' Greek text and smuggled into England in bales of cloth. Though Tyndale was later executed, his vivid phrasing endured, shaping much of the King James New Testament's wording.
events.dateNotes: Printing began in Cologne in 1525 but was stopped by the authorities; the first complete printed English New Testament appeared at Worms in 1526. Tyndale was executed in 1536.

events.name: Calvin Publishes Institutes of the Christian Religion
events.description: John Calvin publishes the first edition of the Institutes in Basel at age 26, expanded in later editions to the definitive 1559 Latin text, which became a foundational statement of Reformed theology.
events.dateNotes: First edition 1536; expanded final edition 1559.

events.name: William Tyndale Executed
events.description: Tyndale is strangled and burned at Vilvoorde near Brussels in October 1536 for translating the Bible into English. His wording largely shaped the King James Version.
events.dateNotes: Early October 1536; the exact day is unknown.

events.name: Ignatius Founds the Jesuits
events.description: Pope Paul III approves the Society of Jesus on 27 September 1540. Founded by Ignatius of Loyola and his companions, it centres on education, missions and obedience to the pope and becomes a major force in Catholic renewal and world missions.
events.dateNotes: Bull Regimini militantis ecclesiae, 27 September 1540.

events.name: Council of Trent
events.description: Meeting in three periods between 1545 and 1563, the Council of Trent defined Catholic doctrine on Scripture, justification and the sacraments, and enacted reforms of clergy and discipline in response to Protestant challenges.
events.dateNotes: Council of Trent, 1545–1563 (three periods over 18 years).

events.name: Francis Xavier Reaches Japan
